Verdict: YES—allow one bounded same-angle retry. The reviewer’s counterexample has the wrong order.

For B=[h,2h], u=1/4, and Q=δ_(h,1,1), p=P(X∈B,A=1)=∫_h^(2h) x²/4 dx=7h³/12. Thus the limiting boundary shift is h(m₁ᴿ(B)-1/2)=hε/[2{(1-ε)(7h³/12)+ε}]. At h=ε^(1/4), this is Θ(h²)=Θ(ε^(1/2)), not Θ(h). The contaminant does not dominate the clean treated mass because ε=h⁴≪h³.

Suggested root directive: Retry angle 0 once, re-centered as a field-tier one-dimensional calibration theorem. Keep the exact declared class d=1, α=β=1, κ=2, and replace the compressed estimator definition by the following total algorithm and contamination lemma. Set b=max{n^(-1/5),ε^(1/4)}. If b>1/4, return 0. Otherwise let h be the smallest dyadic number at least b. Partition [h,1] into dyadic slabs S_j=[r_j,2r_j], r_j=2^j h, and split S_j into M_j=ceil(sqrt(r_j)/h) equal half-open cells, with an explicit endpoint convention. Let B=[h,2h]. For each arm and cell, use the bounded empirical arm mean, defaulting to 1/2 when its denominator is zero. Return clip_[-1/2,1/2][Σ_C |C|{m̂₁(C)-m̂₀(C)}+h{m̂₁(B)-m̂₀(B)}]. No observation below h is used; B extrapolates the missing boundary integral. The estimator is finite and data-only, with O(n log(1/h)+h^(-1)) arithmetic and O(h^(-1)) memory. Prove explicitly sup_(P,Q) E|θ̂-θ(P)| ≤ C_L[h²+(nh)^(-1/2)+εh^(-2)+exp(-cnh^(7/2))]. For a body cell C⊂[r,2r], writing q_C=Q(X∈C,A=a), its weighted contamination shift is at most Cεq_C/r²; summing uses only Σ_C q_C≤1. The extra boundary term is at most Cεq_B/h². Hence both a point contaminant—including an atom at h, even though B and the first body cell reuse it—and arbitrary diffuse within-cell contamination contribute at most Cε/h². No cellwise contamination restriction is assumed. Claim exactly R_n(ε;1,1,1,2,L) ≍_L n^(-2/5)+ε^(1/2), 0≤ε≤1/10. Equivalently, the exact Huber-radius expression uses sqrt(ε/(1-ε)), uniformly equivalent here. Do not claim that the general multidimensional frontier is solved.

Matching same-experiment lower-bound target: take u=1/2, μ₀=1/2, binary outcomes, μ₁,₀=1/2 and μ₁,₁=1/2+a(h-x)_+, a=1/4. Then Δθ=ah²/2, TV(P₀,P₁)=ah⁴/24, and KL(P₁∥P₀)≤a²h⁵/15. With h=n^(-1/5) and Q_k=P_k, the contaminated experiment reduces to the clean pair and gives n^(-2/5). With h≍{ε/(1-ε)}^(1/4), the two Huber neighborhoods intersect, so choose Q₀,Q₁ yielding the identical observed law R; target separation is ≍sqrt(ε/(1-ε)). Taking the maximum gives the claimed sum up to constants.
